title: How a Christian Man Dies
author: Bethel McGrew
summary: Bethel McGrew examines what the death of Senator Ben Sasse reveals about Christian manhood in contrast to the counterfeit masculinity offered by the manosphere streamers featured in Netflix's 'Inside the Manosphere.' The piece begins with the disturbing 'looksmaxxing' trend -- a macabre self-harm regime justified by the mantra 'men aren't supposed to be happy' -- and traces this as a twisted corruption of the genuine call to endure suffering and carry a cross. McGrew argues that figures like Jordan Peterson briefly met the need for a demanding masculine vision but collapsed under their own weight, leaving the field open to far worse substitutes. Against this backdrop, Sasse's death is offered as a counter-example: a man who carried suffering with integrity, humor, and genuine faith, without spectacle. The piece is a theological and cultural meditation on the difference between authentic Christian dying -- and living -- and the manosphere's grim counterfeit of endurance without virtue.
points: * McGrew locates the manosphere's appeal in a genuine truth it corrupts: young men rightly hunger for challenge and meaning, but the manosphere offers suffering stripped of integrity or virtue, producing only pain without transformation. * The 'looksmaxxing' trend represents the most disturbing variation on counterfeit masculinity -- presenting a twisted ascetic mortification as self-improvement while delivering only self-harm and ideological capture. * Jordan Peterson's early success showed what was possible when men were offered a demanding vision of carrying their cross, but his public collapse illustrated the fragility of any masculine ideal not rooted in actual community and grace. * Ben Sasse's death is held up as a genuine example of Christian dying: a man who faced suffering with quiet humor, theological grounding, and without the spectacle that the manosphere mistakes for strength. * The deepest distinction McGrew draws is between suffering that forms character and suffering that merely performs it -- the former produces wisdom and love, the latter produces hardness and exploitation.
quotes: In isolation, one could agree that young Peters is expressing a true saying. As Job says, 'Man is born unto trouble as the sparks fly upward.' I can actually see why certain young men would be drawn to this. They crave an ancient tonic against complacent, soft modernity. They don't want to be carried through life on flowery beds of ease.

But the tortured professor would go on to collapse very publicly under the weight of his own cross. In his absence, all manner of unsavory characters have rushed in, offering lost boys a simulacrum of tough masculinity stripped of anything resembling integrity or virtue.
The looksmaxxing trend is perhaps the most disturbing variation on the theme of snake-oil masculinity, sadder and more twisted even than the decadence sold by an Andrew Tate figure.

There's a moment in the Netflix documentary where Justin Waller talks about how these boys constantly stop him on the street to thank him for 'helping' them. It was a depressing reminder of how often Peterson used to say the same.

One of them reveals that he first moved to Miami to try to 'make it big' when he was wrestling with grief over his brother's suicide. At first, he was living out of his car, 'feeling sorry for myself, crying every night.' Then, he tells us, he had an epiphany: 'Maybe, as men, we're meant to suffer. We're not meant to be happy.'
